title: Adverse health effects of non-medical cannabis use

claims.statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by Connor et al., 2021) or up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study of frequent use (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced. No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, with 17% in its table); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one after stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors read early onset as a marker of other psychiatric and substance use problems rather than a risk factor in itself (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). In a 3-year prospective study of people who used frequently, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14: unadjusted HR 2.47; adjusted 0.63 (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model mood disorder 2.69, personality disorder 2.30, anxiety disorder 2.31, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6), alcohol dependence 2.55.

claims.statement: In US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had at some point met criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 31.9% for tobacco, 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey; among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, with a median of about 5 years from first use to dependence; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). That review cites about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder in more recent US national data, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); tobacco 31.9% (no SE), heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; median time from first use to dependence about 5 years. Second-hand: about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015).

claims.statement: As described in an American Heart Association scientific statement and in narrative reviews (all figures second-hand; no primary study was read here, and the statement gives no search or appraisal method), studies of adults who use cannabis point in different directions on heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood-vessel disease, and the AHA writing group judged the evidence still inconclusive (Page et al., 2020). In the hour after use, the risk of a heart attack starting was 4.8 times that at other times in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, an estimate printed without an interval that rests on the 9 people who had used cannabis in that hour (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015, calls it a quadrupling). Two surveys found more stroke: past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 2.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related factors including tobacco smoking, with the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7; adjustment not stated) (Hemachandra et al., 2016); and among adults aged 18 to 44, use went with an adjusted OR for stroke of 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al.; adjustment set not stated). Health-record and hospital databases report more heart attacks where cannabis use is recorded, for example 1.37% against 0.54% over 3 years (about 14 against 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion; RR 2.53, adjustment not stated; Chami & Kim, 2019), but the statement warns that samples of hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias. Against these, in the CARDIA cohort (5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed for more than 25 years) cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., 2017; no estimates printed), and after a heart attack long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; adjustment not stated; Frost et al., 2013). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate, to which healthy young adults quickly become tolerant, and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Page et al., 2020). The statement names short-term, observational and retrospective designs, poorly measured exposure, recall bias, low-risk cohorts and confounding by tobacco as the main weaknesses, and judges the evidence for people with cardiac risk factors insufficient; Hall (2015) concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: All second-hand. Case-crossover (Mittleman et al. 2001, 3,882 people with a heart attack): onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval; 9 people had used cannabis in that hour); follow-up of 1,913: mortality over 3.8 years 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009). Stroke: Hemachandra et al. 2016, past-year use, rate ratio 3.3 (1.8 to 6.3) unadjusted and 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) adjusted including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1 to 10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al., adults aged 18 to 44, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97) with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46) with e-cigarettes. Databases: Chami & Kim 2019, 3-year heart-attack incidence 1.37% vs 0.54% (about 14 vs 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion), RR 2.53 (2.45 to 2.61); Desai et al. 2019, heart-attack admissions of young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%. CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017, 5,113 adults, over 25 years): no association, no estimates printed. After a heart attack: Frost et al. 2013, mortality 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.05, P = 0.28; Johnson-Sasso et al. 2018, in-hospital mortality OR 0.79. Laboratory: exercise time to angina 48% shorter after one cannabis cigarette than after placebo.

claims.statement: In studies of pregnant women and their newborns published from 1982 to 2014 (24 articles from 19 studies, mostly cohorts; 15 of the 24 articles before 2000, editors' count; English only), any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (women using other illicit drugs left out, but not those who smoked tobacco or drank alcohol), compared with no cannabis use during pregnancy, is associated with somewhat smaller babies and more admissions to intensive care, but not detectably with early birth. In a 2016 meta-analysis whose pooled estimates are crude, with no adjustment stated (Gunn et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low), exposed babies weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (95% CI 39 to 180 g; 10 studies, 4 of them finding lower weight; I2 63%), and had higher odds of weighing under 2,500 g (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, 2 of them positive; I2 89%) and of admission to neonatal or other intensive care (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, 3 positive; I2 78%), while preterm birth before 37 weeks (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies), length of pregnancy, length and head size at birth, Apgar scores, birth defects and deaths around the time of birth showed no clear difference. No absolute risks were reported, and the review does not discuss whether intensive-care admission reflects the babies' health or hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs (editors' observation). Mothers who used cannabis also had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies), a result carried mainly by one large study. The review's authors say that, because most studies did not separate cannabis from tobacco and alcohol, which themselves cause low birth weight and early birth, they cannot tell whether the associations come from cannabis. As described second-hand in narrative reviews and a professional statement: an earlier meta-analysis found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy reduced birth weight, though less than tobacco smoking did, and one large study found no rise in birth defects (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); later large studies reported that the lower birth weight generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, although cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully and self-reported use under-counts use (Hall, 2015); and in one US state with legal cannabis, prenatal use went with 1.5 times the odds of low birth weight after adjustment for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use (OR 1.5, 1.1 to 2.1; Crume et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Gunn et al. 2016 (pooled, no adjustment stated; random effects unless noted): birth weight about 109 g lower in exposed babies (printed as a positive mean difference, 109.42 g, 95% CI 38.72 to 180.12; 10 studies; I2 63%); low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies; I2 89%); NICU or ICU admission OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies; I2 78%); preterm birth OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies; I2 85%); gestational age -0.20 weeks (-0.62 to 0.22; 5 studies; fixed effect); length -0.10 cm (-0.65 to 0.45; 6 studies; I2 59%); head circumference -0.31 cm (-0.74 to 0.13; 6 studies; I2 97%); maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies; fixed effect). No absolute risks reported. As relayed by Page et al. 2020: one later US state study, low birth weight OR 1.5 (1.1 to 2.1) adjusted for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use.

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how much, cannabis use causes psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. The association with later psychosis is consistent and stronger with frequent use (see the answer on how often people use), but in the studies read a substantial part of it is explained by measured confounders, and genetically informed studies suggest that a further part reflects shared family or genetic liability, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely; none of these designs excludes a causal contribution, and none measures the effect of frequent or high-potency use. Adjustment for each cohort's measured confounders removed on average about 45% (10% to 80%) of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts (Moore et al., 2007). In the one co-relative study, a Swedish registry analysis described in a viewpoint whose second author co-wrote it (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the odds ratio for schizophrenia with registry-recorded cannabis misuse fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and to 3.52 (3.92 in the viewpoint's table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, with no significance test at the twin level and the adjustment set not stated. Three two-sample Mendelian randomization studies used genetic variants for having ever used cannabis, which explain about 1% or less of the variation in ever use where this is reported, with no adjustment beyond the source studies in the main analyses. The odds ratio for schizophrenia by genetic liability to ever use was 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07) per doubling of the odds of ever use and 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by the pleiotropy-robust MR-Egger method (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, which its authors rescale to 1.37 for ever against never use (Vaucher et al., 2018); and 1.04 (p = 0.81) with five genome-wide significant variants or 1.10 (0.99 to 1.21) with 69 variants (Pasman et al., 2018). In the reverse direction, genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, Pasman et al., 2018), and the genetic correlation between ever use and schizophrenia was 0.25 (Pasman et al., 2018, as corrected). These three studies share consortium data and are not independent. Narrative reviews read the evidence available to them as shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016), as partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), or as strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Attenuation of the crude association by each cohort's adjustment: about 45% on average (10% to 80%) (Moore et al., 2007). Co-relative (one registry study, misuse): OR 10.44 in the general population, 5.07 in full siblings, 3.52 or 3.92 in discordant identical twins (untested). Mendelian randomization, liability to ever use on schizophrenia: 1.04 (1.01–1.07) per doubling of the odds, MR-Egger 1.01 (0.93–1.10), 12 variants 1.03 (0.99–1.08) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02–1.14) per unit of log odds, rescaled 1.37 (1.09–1.67) ever vs never, 1.41 (1.09–1.83) adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018); 1.04 (p = 0.81) with 5 variants, 1.10 (0.99–1.21) with 69, GSMR 1.21 (p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). Liability to schizophrenia on ever use: 1.10 (1.05–1.14) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017); 1.16 (1.06–1.27) per unit (Pasman et al., 2018). Genetic correlation rg 0.25 (SE 0.03).

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether rates of schizophrenia or psychosis changed as cannabis use rose: the studies that narrative reviews cite disagree, all are ecological, and their figures are second-hand here. As described in the reviews, an Australian modelling study by the reviewers' own group found no clear rise in psychosis incidence after steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a British modelling study judged it too early to see any rise in England and Wales; case-register studies in Britain and Switzerland (south-east London and Zurich) reported rising incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts, and in south-east London incidence of schizophrenia was described as doubling between 1965 and 1999 while the share of patients who had used cannabis rose; a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice found no increase, known only through a 2008 government advisory report (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Murray et al., 2016); and in the UK, according to a commentary cited by a critical overview, cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s without a rise in first admissions for schizophrenia, perhaps with a slight fall (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Reviews that lean towards a causal reading call this weak evidence: individuals' use and illness are not linked, confounders and other changing risk factors are not accounted for, even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and changing diagnostic criteria, services and records could hide or create trends (Gage et al., 2016; Hall, 2015); the 2007 systematic review adds that time lags and unreliable incidence data may hide changes (Moore et al., 2007); the critical overview treats the UK figures as evidence against a causal effect (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Across places rather than over time, in one primary study of 10 sites in Europe and Brazil, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls reported daily use (r about 0.8) or high-potency use (about 0.7), an ecological correlation between two strongly overlapping measures (Di Forti et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimate. As described in reviews: no clear rise in Australia (modelling); too early to detect in England and Wales (modelling); rising incidence in recent birth cohorts in south-east London and Zurich (case registers), with schizophrenia incidence in south-east London described as doubling between 1965 and 1999; no rise in a British general-practice study (third-hand); at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s without a rise in first admissions (from a commentary). Across 10 sites: correlation of adjusted incidence with daily use among controls r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) and with high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286), the two exposures themselves strongly correlated.

claims.statement: In prospective population cohorts from the USA (one with Puerto Rico), Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand that measured cannabis use before age 18 and depression or anxiety later, adolescents in the highest category of use each study reported (mostly self-reported frequency in the past year or 6 months, such as weekly or daily use; in one study a cannabis use disorder by 17), compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis, had modestly higher odds of depression in young adulthood after adjustment for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety and other covariates chosen by each study: in a 2019 meta-analysis (Gobbi et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low) the pooled adjusted OR was 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%), with every study's estimate above 1 (1.02 to 2.62) but only 2 of the 7 significant on their own, and 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67) without a cohort that overlaps with another. Anxiety did not clearly differ (OR 1.18, 0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). No absolute risks were reported, and the review's figure of 7.2% of young-adult depression attributable to cannabis assumes that the link is causal, has no stated method and is not a result of its data. Which pooled estimates were adjusted for tobacco and other drugs cannot be checked from the article, and the authors say a strong causal inference cannot be made; they cite a propensity-score analysis in which the association became non-significant, and among 24 studies they could not pool, six found no association, one of them finding that males with more depressive symptoms went on to use more cannabis and linking later depression to tobacco rather than cannabis. Narrative reviews describe the link with depression as inconsistent and weaker than that with psychosis, with dose–response relations that lost significance after adjustment in one birth cohort (frequency of use by 16) and in the Swedish conscript cohort (heaviest use at 18), and relay an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies with OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94) and weak support for a causal explanation (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; second-hand); another links regular use with anxiety and depression without established causality (Volkow et al., 2014). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Gobbi et al. 2019, pooled adjusted odds ratios (random effects), highest reported use category against no use: depression 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%; study estimates 1.44, 1.50, 1.10, 1.30, 1.48, 2.62 and 1.02); without the overlapping Victorian cohort 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67); by measure, structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) and scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97); by country, USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) and other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). No absolute risks. Second-hand: an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies, depressive disorders OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009 and Hall 2015.

claims.statement: In prospective population cohorts in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, adolescents in the highest category of cannabis use each study reported, compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis, had higher odds of suicidal thoughts and suicide attempts after adjustment at least for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety, but each pooled estimate rests on three studies, two of which in each pool measured the outcome during adolescence rather than in young adulthood as the review intended (Gobbi et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low): suicidal ideation OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.03; I2 0%; the one young-adult estimate 1.10, 0.58 to 2.07) and suicide attempts OR 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84; I2 61%; study estimates 4.81, 6.83 and 1.87, the young-adult one 6.83, 2.04 to 22.90, and the most precise 1.87, 1.09 to 3.22). No absolute risks were reported. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews by the same first author (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015), the wider evidence is mixed: in a New Zealand case–control study of suicide attempts needing hospital care, 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide met criteria for cannabis dependence or abuse against 2% of 1,028 community controls, and adjustment for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence reduced the odds ratio to about 2 (about 9 before adjustment, editors' calculation from the rounded percentages); in prospective studies, a dose–response between frequency of use by 16 and suicide attempts did not survive adjustment, more than weekly use raised reported suicidal ideation in males only in one analysis, cannabis went with self-harm in females only in another, heavy use raised the risk of depression but not of suicide in a fourth, and an earlier meta-analysis found the studies too varied to pool. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Gobbi et al. 2019, pooled adjusted odds ratios (random effects), 3 studies each, highest reported use category against no use: suicidal ideation 1.50 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.03), I2 0%, study estimates 1.40 (0.70 to 2.80), 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07; young adulthood) and 1.74 (1.16 to 2.60); suicide attempts 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), I2 61.3%, study estimates 4.81 (1.82 to 12.66), 6.83 (2.04 to 22.90; young adulthood) and 1.87 (1.09 to 3.22). No absolute risks. Second-hand (Hall & Degenhardt 2009; Hall 2015): case–control study, 16% of 302 against 2% of 1,028; adjusted OR about 2 (about 9 unadjusted, editors' calculation).

claims.statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, depended strongly on where the sample came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32), and the one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518 participants, is about 27.5 in 100 (editors' calculation on the study card). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms within about a week of stopping or cutting down: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and physical symptoms such as headache, sweating or stomach pain (as summarised by Bahji et al., 2020, and Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent, and THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way (Curran et al., 2016); people seeking help to stop most often report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016); and in people without other medical or psychiatric illness withdrawal is described as carrying no serious risk and usually needing only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52; 50 cohorts; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Editors' calculation on the card: 6,470 of 23,518 participants (27.5%). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks.
